citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x_i'=Rx_i+\upsilon t+a_{0}\quad(i=1,\dots,N)$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},\upsilon\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); $\upsilon$ is the boost velocity
denoted by $v$ in that theorem. Define the block-diagonal map
$$R_{N}:=\operatorname{diag}(R,\dots,R):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$$
and the repeated tuples $\bar a_{0}:=(a_{0},\dots,a_{0})$ and
$\bar\upsilon:=(\upsilon,\dots,\upsilon)$ in $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Thus
$R_N x=(Rx_{1},\dots,Rx_{N})$, and the same componentwise rule applies to
velocities and forces; since $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$,
$R_N^{\mathsf T}R_N=I_{3N}$. If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of the
labels in the first frame, then the description of the same worldlines in the second
frame is
$$\eta(t'):=R_{N}x(t'-b)+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_{0}\qquad(t'\in J+b).$$
By clause 2 of the cited theorem, each $\eta_i$ is $C^{2}$ and
$\eta_i''(t')=R\ddot x_i(t'-b)$, so along the motion
$$m_i\eta_i''(t')=R F_i\bigl(t'-b,x(t'-b),\dot x(t'-b)\bigr).$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the force map below. Let $P$ be the inverse affine
transfer from new-frame data to old-frame data,
$$P(t',y,w):=\bigl(t'-b,\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}),\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\bigr).$$
Its preimage of the original domain is
$$D_{*}:=P^{-1}(D)=\{(t',y,w):P(t',y,w)\in D\};$$
it is open because $P$ is a homeomorphism and $D$ is open. Define
$$F_{*}:D_{*}\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad F_{*}(t',y,w):=R_N F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R_N^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}\bigr),\ R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\Bigr).$$
The map $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its state variable:
the transfer and its inverse are affine, and at fixed time they act linearly
on state differences; on compact time intervals their state Lipschitz
constants are uniform, so precomposition preserves the stated regularity of
$F$. The framework
formulates the equation of motion in every inertial frame; a rule that does
not transform by this law is a description tied to the frame in which it was
written, and the framework attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When
$Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of the models of the companion page — the
transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a proper open $Q$ the
transferred position set $R_NQ+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_0$ may depend on
$t'$, and the equation is then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch the mass metric restricts the
Euclidean inner product to $Q$ as in that item.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** on the open ambient set $O$ is a pair of smooth maps
$$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'\times3N},\qquad b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'},\qquad 1\le k'\le3N,$$
with $A(t,x)$ of constant rank $k'$ everywhere in the declared domain,
imposing $A(t,x(t))\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ on a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval, the parameter $t$ is frame time, and $\dot x(t):=x'(t)$ is the componentwise derivative in the convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Equivalently $A(t,x)$ is a linear map
$\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$. Each row's output unit is declared, and
its corresponding component of $b$ has that same unit. The allowed velocities
at $(t,x)$ form the affine set $\{v:A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0\}$; its differences form
$\ker A(t,x)$.

The law is **locally holonomic-equivalent at $(t_0,x_0)$** if on some open
neighbourhood $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times O$ of that point there are a $C^2$
map $g:V\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $D_xg$ of rank $k'$ and a $C^2$ matrix map
$C:V\to\mathbb R^{k'\times k'}$ with $\det C\ne0$ such that
$$A=C\,D_xg,\qquad b=C\,\partial_tg\qquad\text{on }V.$$
Thus the velocity law is locally the derivative of the regular positional
constraints $g(t,x)=\text{constant}$. It is **locally nonholonomic at the
specified point** when no such neighbourhood and pair $(g,C)$ exists; a
nonholonomic model in this local sense declares a point (or a region of
points) with this failure. For a homogeneous time-independent law this
excludes local position submanifolds whose tangent spaces equal $\ker A$;
for an affine time-dependent law the criterion also includes the drift $b$.
Absence of a single global pair alone does not establish local
nonintegrability. The rank of $A$ counts instantaneous velocity restrictions,
not the dimension of a positional configuration manifold; accessibility
requires its own definition. Rank changes require a separate model.

Adopt the force branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$ particle
labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, a nondegenerate open time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), identify
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}=\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the position
tuple of the labels ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and let $\mathsf M$ be the
mass operator of clause (d) of that definition, $\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N})$, a symmetric positive definite linear map with
block-diagonal matrix and blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$. All components below are read in
this frame, and dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]].

**(a) Constraint datum.** A **holonomic-constraint datum** on this data is a
triple $(O,k,G)$ with:

1. an **ambient set** $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, open and
   nonempty;
2. an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le 3N-1$;
3. a map $G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\to\mathbb R^{k}$ of class $C^{2}$
   ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), each component carrying a
   declared dimension $[G_{\alpha}]=\gamma_{\alpha}$ fixed by the model (the
   model may rescale a component by a nonzero constant, which changes
   $\gamma_{\alpha}$ and the component but not its zero set);

subject to the two hypotheses

4. **nonempty admissible locus:** the **constraint locus**
   $$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x)\in O:\ G(t,x)=0\bigr\}$$
   is nonempty and contained in $I_{0}\times Q$: every constrained
   configuration is an admissible configuration of the force-branch model and
   every constrained time lies in its time window;
5. **regularity:** for every $(t,x)\in\Sigma$ the Jacobian $D_{x}G(t,x)$
   ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) is surjective, equivalently has rank
   $k$.

For $t\in\mathbb R$ write $\Sigma_{t}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:(t,x)\in\Sigma\}$
for the **instantaneous constraint locus**. If $\Sigma_{t}\neq\varnothing$,
then $x\mapsto G(t,x)$ has the regular value $0$ with nonempty fibre
$\Sigma_{t}$ in the sense of [[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]
(on the open set $\{x:(t,x)\in O\}$), so by
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] the set $\Sigma_{t}$ is
an embedded submanifold of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$
([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]); when $k=3N-1$ the
instantaneous locus is locally a curve, and the number
$$\dim\Sigma_{t}=3N-k$$
is the **instantaneous degrees of freedom** of the constrained branch. The
set $V(t,x):=\ker D_{x}G(t,x)\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ has dimension $3N-k$ by
the rank-nullity theorem for matrices ([[cor-matrix-rank-nullity]]) and is called the space of **virtual displacements** of the datum
at $(t,x)$; its elements are the first-order differences of constrained
configurations at fixed time, in the sense of the mathematical definition
[[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]. A vector
$v\in\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a **permitted velocity** at $(t,x)\in O$ when
$$G_{t}(t,x)+D_{x}G(t,x)\,v=0 .$$

**(b) Constrained curve families.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). A **constrained curve family** of the
datum is a map $x:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ of class $C^{2}$ with
$(t,x(t))\in O$ and $G(t,x(t))=0$ for every $t\in J$; writing
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with coordinate curves $x_{i}:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ and
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$, the componentwise derivatives of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]];
$w_{i}$ is the coordinate velocity of label $i$), the chain rule
([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) applied to $t\mapsto G(t,x(t))$
gives
$$G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\,w(t)=0\qquad(t\in J),$$
so the velocity of a $C^{1}$ constrained curve family is permitted at every
time. A tuple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})\in O\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ is **consistent
data** of the datum when $G(t_{0},x_{0})=0$ and
$G_{t}(t_{0},x_{0})+D_{x}G(t_{0},x_{0})v_{0}=0$; these are the initial data at
which constrained motions are posed below.

**(c) Reaction field and the constrained equation.** A **reaction field along
a curve family** $x:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a continuous map
$R:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, of force dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ in each
component. The **equation of the constrained datum along $x$** is
$$\mathsf M\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)+R(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
componentwise $m_{i}x_{i}''(t)=F_{i}(t,x(t),w(t))+R_{i}(t)$. A
**holonomic-constraint model** consists of the force-branch data, a
holonomic-constraint datum $(O,k,G)$, and the declaration that the position
tuple of the labels satisfies $G(t,x(t))=0$ for all times while a reaction
field acts: a **constrained motion** of the model (with reaction $R$) is a
constrained curve family $x:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ together with a reaction field
$R$ satisfying the displayed equation. The force map $F$ is the model's
declared interaction force of the force branch, and $R$ is the additional
force contribution exerted by the mechanism that realizes the constraint; the
total force along a constrained motion is the pointwise sum $F+R$ in the sense
of clause (v) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]], read along the curve. The
reaction is **not** part of the force map: the constrained branch is the branch
excluded by clause (i) of that postulate, and the equation above is the
adopted equation of the constrained model. For any specified constrained curve
family $x$, this equation fixes the reaction uniquely as the residual field
$$R(t)=\mathsf Mx''(t)-F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr).$$
Without an additional reaction law, the constraint and this equation do not
select which constrained curve families are dynamically admissible: every
$C^{2}$ constrained curve can be paired with its continuous residual field to
satisfy the equation. The ideal-reaction law of the postulate of this page is
the additional model assumption that selects among these candidates by
requiring the reaction to annihilate the virtual displacements.

**(d) Scleronomic and rheonomic constraints.** The datum is **scleronomic**
when the constraint locus is time-independent, in the precise sense that there
is a set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with
$$\Sigma=\bigl\{(t,x)\in O:\ x\in N\bigr\};$$
equivalently, membership in the locus is a condition on $x$ alone within $O$:
if $(t,x)\in\Sigma$ and $(t',x)\in O$, then $(t',x)\in\Sigma$ (the two
formulations are exchanged by passing between $N$ and the projection of
$\Sigma$ to $\mathbb R^{3N}$). For the standard product ambient set
$O=I_{0}\times Q$ the condition reads $\Sigma=I_{0}\times(N\cap Q)$. The datum
is **rheonomic** otherwise.

If the datum is scleronomic, then the declared presentation $G$, and every
$C^{2}$ presentation of the same locus with the rank hypothesis, satisfy
$$G_{t}(t,x)=0\qquad\text{for every }(t,x)\in\Sigma,$$
because for $x\in N$ every $(t,x)\in O$ lies in $\Sigma$, so $t\mapsto G(t,x)$
vanishes identically on the open set of times $\{t:(t,x)\in O\}$; this is the
form in which the classification is used by the balance theorems of this page.

The identity is a consequence of time-independence and **not** a criterion for
it. The presentation $G(t,x):=(x_{1}-t)^{2}$ on
$O=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ has the moving zero set $\{x_{1}=t\}$ while
$G_{t}(t,x)=-2(x_{1}-t)$ vanishes at every point of that set; this presentation
violates the rank hypothesis, but the identity can also hold for a
rank-regular presentation: on
$O=\bigl((0,1)\cup(2,3)\bigr)\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ the $C^{2}$ map equal to
$x_{1}$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and to $1$ on
$(2,3)\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ has the rank-$1$ zero set
$\Sigma=(0,1)\times\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:x_{1}=0\}$ with $G_{t}=0$ on $\Sigma$,
yet $\Sigma$ is not of the form $\{(t,x)\in O:x\in N\}$ for any $N$: the point
$(1/2,0)\in\Sigma$ would force $0\in N$, and then $(5/2,0)\in O$ would lie in
$\Sigma$. Hence the classification is a property of the locus, and the
identity is used only in the direction proved above.

Under a nowhere-vanishing $C^{2}$ rescaling $G'=\rho G$ one has
$D_{x}G'=\rho\,D_{x}G$ and $G'_{t}=\rho_{t}G+\rho G_{t}=\rho G_{t}$ at the
points of $\Sigma$, so the virtual displacements and permitted velocities are
unchanged, the multiplier of a motion transforms as
$\lambda'=\rho^{-1}\lambda$, and the reaction $D_{x}G'^{\mathsf T}\lambda'$
and the product $-\lambda'\cdot G'_{t}=-\lambda\cdot G_{t}$ of the rheonomic
power theorem are unchanged at the locus.

**(e) Status.** This item defines a model class: it fixes the constraint
datum, the constrained curves, the virtual displacements, the reaction field
and the equation of the constrained branch. It adopts no ideal-reaction law
(that is the content of the ideal-reaction postulate of this page), no particular force
law, and no measured value. Whether a concrete apparatus — a frictionless
joint, a smooth track, a taut rod or string, a no-slip contact — is described
by a holonomic-constraint model is an application-level judgement recorded with
the apparatus, together with the regime in which the rigidity, frictionlessness
or contact assumptions are adequate; the framework itself attaches no empirical
claim to the class.

Adopt as a physical assumption of the framework, in the setting of
[[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]]:

**(i) The ideal-reaction law.** Along every constrained motion $x:J\to
\mathbb R^{3N}$ of a holonomic-constraint model, with reaction field
$R:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, the reaction annihilates every virtual displacement:

$$R(t)\cdot\delta=0\qquad\text{for every }t\in J\text{ and every }\delta\in V\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)=\ker D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),$$

the pairing being the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). This is the **d'Alembert condition** (the
condition of zero virtual work of the reaction) in the sense of
[[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]. By the multiplier lemma
[[lem-cm-constraint-multipliers-and-accelerations]], applied at each time with
the surjective Jacobian $D_{x}G(t,x(t))$, the condition holds at time $t$ if
and only if there is a unique $\lambda(t)\in\mathbb R^{k}$ with
$$R(t)=D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t);$$
this representation is a mathematical consequence of the condition and the
rank hypothesis, not a separate assumption, and the multiplier has dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}/\gamma_{\alpha}$ in component $\alpha$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The condition is imposed only along the motions of the
model, and it does not by itself determine $R$: it constrains $R$ at each time
to the $k$-dimensional conormal space, and which element occurs is fixed by
the twice-differentiated constraint through the balance theorem of this page.

**(ii) What is adopted.** Clause (i) is an adopted restriction on the
mechanism that realizes the constraint, not a theorem about bodies, tracks or
contacts. It is the idealization of a mechanism that exerts only the reaction
needed to maintain the constraint, distributed normally to the admissible
directions at each instant; the force branch of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] excludes constraint reactions from its force
maps, and this postulate is the additional law that closes the constrained
branch.

**(iii) Intended model identifications.** The framework intends clause (i) to
model, subject to the qualifications of clause (iv): frictionless hinges and
joints; smooth bilateral contacts and tracks; a taut light rod, and a taut
string while it stays taut; and no-slip rolling in the planar holonomic case,
provided the contact can supply the required tangential reaction. Each of
these identifications is an application-level statement made and recorded with
the apparatus; the framework asserts no measurement, no material parameter and
no numerical value here.

**(iv) Limits of the idealization.** The law is **not** asserted for:

1. constraints with dry sliding friction along an admissible direction, whose
   force has a component doing virtual work on admissible displacements — such
   friction must be declared as a separate force contribution with its own
   model;
2. unilateral contacts and mechanisms that can release the constraint (a bead
   on the outside of a surface, a string that can go slack, a block that can
   separate), which are maintained only while the required reaction satisfies
   a one-sided capability condition; where the condition fails, the constraint
   is released and a contact-change model is required, and none is supplied
   here;
3. points where the Jacobian $D_{x}G$ drops rank, which lie outside the
   regularity hypothesis of the datum and outside the representation above;
4. active mechanisms that drive the constraint (motors, moving walls driven by
   external equipment): their driving must be declared as an additional force
   contribution, and the ideal reaction then accounts only for the passive
   maintenance of the constraint;
5. any claim that the mechanism can mechanically supply the computed
   reaction: the law computes the reaction the ideal constraint exerts; whether
   a physical contact, rod or string can supply it (friction cone, sign of a
   tensile force, strength limits, no-slip conditions) is an additional
   premise of an application.

**(v) The law is not a work statement.** Clause (i) concerns virtual
displacements at fixed time; it does not assert that the reaction performs no
work along the motion. For a scleronomic constraint the reaction power
vanishes identically, but for a rheonomic constraint the reaction can do work,
with $R\cdot x'=-\lambda\cdot G_{t}$; the precise statement, its static case
and worked models are the content of the rheonomic-power theorem and the
companion examples of this page.

**(vi) Status and empirical content.** The clause is adopted, not deduced; the
sources record the ideal-reaction condition as an additional physical
hypothesis attached to a constraint, not as a consequence of writing the
constraint down. The passage from clause (i) to the constrained equation of
motion is a theorem with explicit regularity hypotheses, proved on this page.
Whether the idealization is adequate for a given apparatus is decided by
comparing the model's conditional predictions with reported observations under
the stated regime, with the qualifications of clause (iv) carried along;
agreement of such a comparison is evidence about the combined model and
apparatus, not a proof of the idealization.

Adopt a holonomic-constraint model of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]]
with datum $(O,k,G)$, mass operator $\mathsf M$, force map $F$, and the
ideal-reaction law of [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]]. Suppose, in addition
to the hypotheses of those items:

**(h1)** $G$ is of class $C^{3}$ on $O$, and $D_{x}G(t,x)$ has rank $k$ for
every $(t,x)\in O$ (not only on the constraint locus);

**(h2)** the force map is of class $C^{1}$ on
$I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).

Set $O':=O\cap(I_{0}\times Q)$. This is an open nonempty set because
$\Sigma\subseteq O'$ and $\Sigma$ is nonempty. The matrix-valued map
$C:O\to M_{k}(\mathbb R)$ below is defined on $O$, while
$\Lambda:O'\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$ and
$a:O'\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ are defined on the
force-map domain restricted to the constraint datum; this is the time-state
domain of the first-order system. Every constrained motion in the statement has
$(t,x(t))\in\Sigma\subseteq O'$, so these functions are defined along it.

Let $x:J\to Q$ be a constrained motion of the model with reaction field $R$
satisfying the ideal-reaction law, on an interval $J\subseteq I_{0}$ with
nonempty interior, and write $w=x'$ for its velocity. Then:

1. **multiplier form.** For every $t\in J$ there is a unique
   $\lambda(t)\in\mathbb R^{k}$ with $R(t)=D_{x}G(t,x(t))^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t)$;
   the map $\lambda:J\to\mathbb R^{k}$ so defined is continuous, and with

$$C(t,x):=D_{x}G(t,x)\,\mathsf M^{-1}D_{x}G(t,x)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \Lambda(t,x,v):=-C(t,x)^{-1}\Bigl[D_{x}G\,\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)+G_{tt}+2G_{tq}[v]+G_{qq}[v,v]\Bigr],$$

   the terms being evaluated at $(t,x)$ or $(t,x,v)$, the $k\times k$ matrix
   $C(t,x)$ is symmetric positive definite and invertible and
   $$\lambda(t)=\Lambda\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J):$$
   the multiplier, and hence the reaction, is determined by the model data
   and the motion, not a free or measured quantity.

2. **determined dynamics.** With
   $a(t,x,v):=\mathsf M^{-1}\bigl(F(t,x,v)+D_{x}G(t,x)^{\mathsf T}\Lambda(t,x,v)\bigr)$,
   the tuple $(x,w)$ solves the first-order system
   $$x'=v,\qquad v'=a(t,x,v)$$
   on $J$; conversely every solution $(x,v)$ of this system on an interval
   whose initial datum is consistent, with
   $R(t):=D_{x}G(t,x(t))^{\mathsf T}\Lambda(t,x(t),v(t))$, is a constrained
   motion of the model satisfying the ideal-reaction law; and through every
   consistent datum $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ there is a unique maximal solution
   of the system. Hence the holonomic-constraint model with ideal reactions
   has determined dynamics on its constraint locus.

3. **preservation.** Along every solution of clause 2 with consistent data,
   $$G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)=0,\qquad G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)v(t)=0$$
   for every $t$ of its maximal interval.

4. **reaction power.** Along every ideal constrained motion as in clause 1,
   $$R(t)\cdot w(t)=-\lambda(t)\cdot G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J),$$
   the pairings being the Euclidean inner products.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and ideal-reaction
law and on hypotheses (h1)-(h2); it asserts no empirical value, and the
multiplier is a representation tied to the declared components of $G$.

Adopt a holonomic-constraint model of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]]
with datum $(O,k,G)$ and the ideal-reaction law of
[[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]]. Suppose, in addition to the model
hypotheses, that $G$ is of class $C^{3}$ on $O$ and $D_{x}G(t,x)$ has rank
$k$ for every $(t,x)\in O$, and that the force map is of class $C^{1}$ on
$I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; these are hypotheses (h1)-(h2) of
[[pthm-cm06-multiplier-balance]]. Let
$x:J\to Q$ be a constrained motion with ideal reaction $R$ on an interval
$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior, with velocity $w=x'$ and multiplier
$\lambda:J\to\mathbb R^{k}$ as in [[pthm-cm06-multiplier-balance]] clause 1.
Suppose further that the model's force map is presented through a potential
with residual forces in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]: a $C^{2}$ function
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and maps
$d_{i}:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3}$ with the
standing regularity of clause (iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]], such
that
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
on the state domain ([[def-cm01-units]] for the dimensions). Write
$K$ and $E(t):=K(t)+U(t,x(t))$ for the kinetic and mechanical energy of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]] clauses (b),(d) and of clause (b) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]], and
$\mathfrak d_{i}(t):=d_{i}(t,x(t),w(t))$ for the evaluated residual forces.
Then:

1. **reaction power and reaction work.** For every $t\in J$,
   $$R(t)\cdot w(t)=-\lambda(t)\cdot G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),$$
   and for all $t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$, $\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}R(t)\cdot w(t)\,dt
   =-\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\lambda(t)\cdot G_{t}(t,x(t))\,dt$. If the datum is
   scleronomic, then $R\cdot w\equiv0$ on $J$ and the reaction performs no
   work over any subinterval.

2. **mechanical-energy balance.** $E$ is differentiable on $J$ and
   $$E'(t)=\partial_{t}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+\sum_{i}\bigl\langle\mathfrak d_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle-\lambda(t)\cdot G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J):$$
   the mechanical energy changes at the rate of the explicit time dependence
   of the potential, the power of the residual forces, and the constraint
   term $-\lambda\cdot G_{t}$, which vanishes identically for a scleronomic
   constraint.

3. **conservation in the static scleronomic case.** If the datum is
   scleronomic, $\partial_{t}U\equiv0$ on $I_{0}\times Q$, and
   $\mathfrak d_{i}\equiv0$ for every $i$ along the motion, then $E$ is
   constant on $J$.

4. **integrated work form.** For all $t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$,
   $$K(t_{1})-K(t_{0})=U\bigl(t_{0},x(t_{0})\bigr)-U\bigl(t_{1},x(t_{1})\bigr)+\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\Bigl[\partial_{t}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+\sum_{i}\bigl\langle\mathfrak d_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle-\lambda(t)\cdot G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\Bigr]dt .$$

The constraint term of clause 2 is not a force of the model's force map: it is
the mechanical work performed by the ideal mechanism that maintains a
time-dependent constraint, and clause 1 records that this work is exactly the
virtual-work-free reaction's actual power. The statement is conditional on the
adopted model, idealization and potential presentation; it asserts no measured
value.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], with configuration domain $Q$, time
window $I_{0}$ and force map $F$. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]]
and gradients are Euclidean ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); points of
$Q$ are written $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$.

**(a) Potential representation of the force map.** A model **presents its
force map through a potential** when it declares a function
$$U:I_{0}\times Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
of class $C^{2}$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules), with
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; here $\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is the
gradient of $u\mapsto U(t,x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},u,x_{i+1},\dots,x_{N})$ at
$u=x_{i}$. More generally, a model may declare **residual forces**
$d_{i}:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of the standing
regularity of clause (iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and present
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v);$$
the pair $(U,d)$ is then the model's presentation and
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}:=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is its **potential part**. The scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** for the model's potential part; the framework's
earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

**(b) Potential and mechanical energy along a curve family.** For a curve
family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

**(d) Closed and exact force fields.** A **time- and velocity-independent
configuration-space force field** is a $C^{1}$ map
$\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{N}):Q\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$, where
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is the open configuration domain and each
$\varphi_i(x)$ is the force on label $i$ at configuration $x$; its components
have force dimension. It represents a force map of the form
$F_i(t,x,v)=\varphi_i(x)$ on the model's state domain. This configuration-space
field is not in general an external single-label force: to identify its
$i$th component with an external map of [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i),
one must further require that it depend on $x_i$ alone, as in the declared
signature $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x_i,v_i)$. Such a field is **closed** when
$\partial_{k}\varphi_{j}=\partial_{j}\varphi_{k}$ for all coordinate indices
$j,k\in\{1,\dots,3N\}$ at every point of $Q$, and **exact with potential
energy $U$** when $\varphi=-\nabla U$ for a $C^{2}$ function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$; equivalently, the field $-\varphi$ is exact in the sense
of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] with potential $U$. The following
mathematical facts are used, with their proofs at the cited items:

1. every exact field is closed, by equality of mixed partial derivatives
   ([[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]);
2. on a star-shaped open domain every closed $C^{1}$ field is exact, by the
   Poincaré lemma ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]);
3. beyond item 2 this item asserts **no** implication from closedness to
   global exactness: on a general open domain a closed field need not have a
   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as
   defined above.

Consequently the existence of a global potential energy on the model's
configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved
energy on every star-shaped subpart of that domain.

**(e) Local potentials.** Let $V\subseteq Q$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to one of its points ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let
$\varphi$ be closed on $V$. Then item 2 of (d) provides a $C^{2}$ potential
$U_{V}:V\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi|_{V}=-\nabla U_{V}$: a **local potential**
of the field on $V$. On the restricted configuration domain $V$ the model
with force $-\nabla U_{V}$ is a global potential model, so the mechanical
energy $K+U_{V}$ is available along curve families in $V$; this is how a
potential is recovered from a merely closed field on a sufficiently small
star-shaped piece of the domain, with no claim of a global representative.

**(f) Equipotential level sets.** Let $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ be $C^{2}$, let
$c\in\mathbb R$ and suppose $U^{-1}(c)\neq\varnothing$ and $\nabla
U(x)\neq0$ for every $x\in U^{-1}(c)$; equivalently $c$ is a regular value of
$U$ and every point of the level set is a regular point
([[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]). Then $U^{-1}(c)$ is an
embedded submanifold of $Q$ of dimension $3N-1$
([[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]],
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]). No such conclusion is made at a
level where $\nabla U$ vanishes somewhere on the level set, where the level
set may have singular points.

**(g) Status.** The potential, its normalization, the residual forces and the
declaration of a potential presentation are model data; the closed/exact
statements of (d)-(f) are cited mathematics about the declared field. This
item asserts no conservation law, no force law of nature and no measured
value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

The locus is $\Sigma=\{(t,r\cos\Omega t,r\sin\Omega t,0):t,r\in\mathbb R\}$, nonempty and contained in $I_{0}	imes Q$, and the virtual displacements at $(t,x)$ are the one-dimensional space $\mathbb R(\cos\Omega t,\sin\Omega t,0)$ because $\delta\in\ker D_{x}G$ means $\delta_{z}=0$ and $-\delta_{x}\sin\Omega t+\delta_{y}\cos\Omega t=0$. Finally the datum is not scleronomic: $(0,(1,0,0))\in\Sigma$ because $G(0,1,0,0)=(0,0)$, while for $t_{1}:=\pi/(2\Omega)$ one has $G_{1}(t_{1},1,0,0)=-\sin(\pi/2)=-1
e0$, so $(t_{1},(1,0,0))\in O=\mathbb R	imes\mathbb R^{3}$ but $(t_{1},(1,0,0))
otin\Sigma$; by the membership form of [F2] the datum is rheonomic.

Consistency of the data: $G(0,x_{0})=(0,0)$ and, with the declared vector $\mathbf v_{0}=(u_{0},\Omega r_{0},0)$, $$G_{t}(0,x_{0})+D_{x}G(0,x_{0})\mathbf v_{0}=(-\Omega r_{0},0)+(\Omega r_{0},0)=(0,0).$$ Thus $(0,x_{0},\mathbf v_{0})$ is consistent.

The curve $x$ is a constrained motion with the stated multiplier: for $r(t)=Ae^{\Omega t}+Be^{-\Omega t}$ one has $r''=\Omega^{2}r$ by [F5], and the displayed $x$ is $C^{\infty}$ with $$x'=r'(\cos\Omega t,\sin\Omega t,0)+r\Omega(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0),\qquad x''=(r''-\Omega^{2}r)(\cos\Omega t,\sin\Omega t,0)+2\Omega r'(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0)=2\Omega r'(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0).$$ Moreover $G(t,x(t))=(-r\cos\Omega t\sin\Omega t+r\sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t,\,0)=(0,0)$, and $G_{t}(t,x(t))+D_{x}G(t,x(t))x'(t)=(-\Omega r,0)+(r\Omega,0)=(0,0)$, so $x$ is a constrained curve family with permitted velocity. With $\lambda(t):=(2m\Omega r'(t),mg)$, the reaction $R:=D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ is $2m\Omega r'(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0)+mg\,e_{3}$, and $F+D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\lambda=(0,0,-mg)+2m\Omega r'(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0)+(0,0,mg)=m\bigl(2\Omega r'(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0)\bigr)=m\,x''=\mathsf Mx''$; since $R=D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ annihilates $\ker D_{x}G$ by [F3], the reaction is ideal and $x$ is a constrained motion of the model with reaction $R$.

The multiplier of step 2.1 is the multiplier $\Lambda$ of the balance theorem and the motion is the unique maximal one: here $C=D_{x}G\,\mathsf M^{-1}D_{x}G^{\mathsf T}=(1/m)I_{2}$ because the two rows of $D_{x}G$ are orthonormal, $D_{x}G\,\mathsf M^{-1}F=(1/m)(0,-mg)=(0,-g)$, $G_{tt}=(-\Omega^{2}G_{1},0)=(0,0)$ along the motion, $2G_{tq}[x']=\bigl(-2\Omega(\cos\Omega t\,x_1'+\sin\Omega t\,x_2'),0\bigr)=(-2\Omega r',0)$ and $G_{qq}[x',x']=0$; hence $\Lambda=-C^{-1}\bigl[(0,-g)+0+(-2\Omega r',0)+0\bigr]=(2m\Omega r',mg)=\lambda$, so by [F3] clause 1 the multiplier of the motion is exactly $\lambda$. Here $O^{\prime}=O=I_{0}\times Q$, $G$ is smooth with rank $2$ throughout $O$ by step 1.1, and $F$ is $C^{1}$ by [F1], so all hypotheses of [F3] hold. The data of step 1.2 are consistent, the curve solves its first-order system, and a solution defined on all of $\mathbb R$ is the maximal solution through its datum by uniqueness.

Reaction power and energy balance: on the motion, $e_{3}\cdot x'=0$ and $(-\sin\Omega t,\cos\Omega t,0)\cdot x'=r\Omega$, so $R\cdot x'=2m\Omega r'\cdot r\Omega=2m\Omega^{2}rr'$, and $G_{t}(t,x(t))=(-\Omega r,0)$ gives $-\lambda\cdot G_{t}=-(2m\Omega r')(-\Omega r)=2m\Omega^{2}rr'$, in agreement with [F4] clause 1. Since $F=-\nabla U$ for $U(t,x,y,z)=mgz$ with residual forces zero and $\partial_{t}U=0$, [F4] clause 2 gives $E'=\partial_{t}U-\lambda\cdot G_{t}=2m\Omega^{2}rr'$. Independently $K'=m(r'r''+\Omega^{2}rr')=m(\Omega^{2}rr'+\Omega^{2}rr')=2m\Omega^{2}rr'$ by [F5], and $z\equiv0$, so $E'=K'=R\cdot x'$. Because the datum is rheonomic (step 1.1), clause 3 of [F4] is not available and the mechanical energy is not asserted constant.

Finite model data: with $m=1$, $\Omega=2$, $r_{0}=1$ and $u_{0}=0$ one has $A=B=\tfrac12$, so $r(t)=\bigl(e^{2t}+e^{-2t}\bigr)/2$, $r'(t)=\bigl(e^{2t}-e^{-2t}\bigr)$, $K(t)=\tfrac12\bigl(r'^{2}+4r^{2}\bigr)=e^{4t}+e^{-4t}$ and $E(t)=K(t)\ \mathrm J$ because $z(t)=0$; then $E'(t)=4\bigl(e^{4t}-e^{-4t}\bigr)\ \mathrm W$, while the reaction power at the same time is $2m\Omega^{2}rr'=8r(t)r'(t)=\tfrac12\cdot8\bigl(e^{2t}+e^{-2t}\bigr)\bigl(e^{2t}-e^{-2t}\bigr)=4\bigl(e^{4t}-e^{-4t}\bigr)$, and the two agree. At $t=\tfrac12\,\mathrm s$ the values are $E=\bigl(e^{2}+e^{-2}\bigr)\approx7.524391\ \mathrm J$, $E'=4\bigl(e^{2}-e^{-2}\bigr)\approx29.014883\ \mathrm W>0$, and $E(0)=2\ \mathrm J$; the energy has increased by the work of the ideal reaction.

Clauses (1)-(4) of the Example are proved: the datum is regular and rheonomic, the data are consistent, the displayed curve is the unique maximal constrained motion with the stated multiplier and reaction, the reaction power is $2m\Omega^{2}rr'$, the mechanical-energy balance holds with the rheonomic term and no other contribution, and the finite model data exhibit a strict energy increase. The construction is an idealization of a bead threaded on a smooth rigid wire whose rotation is prescribed: friction, wire flexibility, driving details and the ability of the wire to supply the computed reaction are not modelled, and the numbers are model values, not measurements of any apparatus.

boundaries.reason: The rotating-wire Example fixes one bead and exactly two constraint components: displacement transverse to the wire and height. The locus contains its explicit rotating radial trajectory; neither a missing label nor an empty constraint family is allowed.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 evaluates the declared zero initial radial velocity and obtains equal exponential coefficients; the first multiplier and reaction power vanish initially. The positive wire speed and mass denominators remain nonzero by the Example hypotheses.

Step 1.1 treats one particle with rank two in three spatial dimensions and computes its one-dimensional radial virtual-displacement space. There is one bead, while replacing the two constraints by one is outside the specified datum.

Step 1.1 proves the wire-normal row and vertical row are independent at every time, including zero radial position. The Example excludes zero mass and zero angular speed; zero radial velocity and a crossing through the origin do not lower this Jacobian rank.

Step 3.1 identifies the explicit exponential trajectory as the maximal motion on all real times. Step 5.1 evaluates time zero and one half second within that domain, so no finite maximal endpoint has been silently crossed.

boundaries.reason: The wire trajectory coefficients A and B are the explicit functions of the prescribed radius and radial velocity in the Example. Step 3.1 identifies its unique multiplier; neither trajectory nor reaction is selected arbitrarily.

The rotating-wire Example verifies its particular constrained exponential trajectory and the energy it receives from the driven wire; it asserts no equivalence between all energy-increasing motions and this wire datum.

The rotating-wire computation does not infer the constraint geometry from an energy increase. Its unique motion is verified from the prescribed rotating straight-wire equations, not by a converse criterion.

risk_review.notes: Checked full model and all seven proof steps. Independent rows (-sin,cos,0) and e3 give rank2 on all O; constraints rotate and are not time-independent. Consistent initial velocity is (u0,Omega r0,0). rsecond=Omega²r gives smooth entire solution even if radial coordinate crosses0; wire is full line, no division by r. Reaction lambda=(2mOmega rprime,mg), and C=(1/m)I2, curvature term zero on locus and mixed term=(-2Omega rprime,0) agree. Corrected missing TeX backslashes and scalar/vector equality typing in proof1.2/2.1/3.1. C3/rank/C1 supplier hypotheses hold, unique entire solution maximal. Eprime=2mOmega²rrprime, finite E(1/2)=7.524391J and Eprime=29.014883W with declared parameters, no measured precision. Rheonomic energy may be constant for some other data; this example asserts an increase only for specified data. Prescribed driven wire and reaction capability are explicitly idealized, not empirical conclusions.

citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),
