citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, let
$G:O\to\mathbb R^k$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and write $G_q(t,q)$ for the Jacobian matrix of
$q\mapsto G(t,q)$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a $k\times n$ matrix. The constraint

$$G(t,q)=0$$

is **regular** when

$$G_q(t,q)\ \text{has rank }k\ \text{for every }(t,q)\in O,$$

equivalently when $G_q$ is surjective at every point ([[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]).
Under this hypothesis each fibre $G(t,\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is a regular level set and every point of it
is a regular point in the sense of [[def-regular-critical-points-values-and-level-sets]].

**Constraint set and admissible data.** Fix a symmetric positive definite matrix
$M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$, meaning $M^{\mathsf T}=M$ and $u^{\mathsf T}Mu>0$ for every $0\ne u\in\mathbb R^n$, and a continuous map
$f:O\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$, the **given force**. A map $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ on an open
interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) is a **constrained curve** when

$$(t,q(t))\in O,\qquad G\bigl(t,q(t)\bigr)=0\qquad(t\in I).$$

**Virtual displacements and permitted velocities.** For $(t,q)\in O$ the **virtual displacements**
at $(t,q)$ are the elements of the kernel

$$V(t,q):=\ker G_q(t,q)=\bigl\{\delta\in\mathbb R^n:G_q(t,q)\delta=0\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n,$$

the tangent space to the level set of $G(t,\cdot)$ at $q$ in the sense of
[[def-tangent-space-to-a-regular-level-set]]; a **permitted velocity** at $(t,q)$ is a vector
$v\in\mathbb R^n$ with

$$G_t(t,q)+G_q(t,q)v=0 .$$

For a $C^1$ constrained curve the differentiated constraint forces
$G_t(t,q(t))+G_q(t,q(t))q'(t)=0$, so its velocity is automatically permitted; the permitted
condition is stated separately because it is the correct initial condition for the first-order
system below.

**Ideal-constraint motions.** A $C^2$ constrained curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ is an
**ideal-constraint motion** of the data $(G,M,f)$ when

1. $q'(t)$ is a permitted velocity at $(t,q(t))$ for every $t\in I$, and
2. there is a continuous map $\lambda:I\to\mathbb R^k$ with

$$Mq''(t)=f\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)+G_q\bigl(t,q(t)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t)\qquad(t\in I).$$

The vector field $R(t):=Mq''(t)-f(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is the **reaction** and
$R=G_q^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ is its **multiplier form**. Since
$G_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T}\lambda\cdot\delta=\lambda\cdot G_q(t,q)\delta=0$ for every
$\delta\in V(t,q)$, every ideal-constraint motion satisfies the **d'Alembert condition**

$$\bigl(Mq''(t)-f(t,q(t),q'(t))\bigr)\cdot\delta=0\qquad\text{for every }\delta\in V(t,q(t)),$$

i.e. the reaction performs no virtual work; the converse implication, that every curve satisfying
the d'Alembert condition is an ideal-constraint motion with a *unique* multiplier, together with
uniqueness of the resulting acceleration, is the content of
[[lem-cm-constraint-multipliers-and-accelerations]] and is not assumed here.

**Scope.** The definition is chartwise and time-dependent: the constraint may depend on $t$
(rheonomic case), its velocity condition is the fixed-time linearisation recorded above, and no
relation between the *variational* (vakonomic) treatment of the constraint and the present
d'Alembert law is asserted. The construction and long-time behaviour of solutions is the subject of
[[prop-cm-ideal-holonomic-system-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]. For a holonomic constraint written
in a chart, the multiplier $\lambda$ is not a measured quantity: only the reaction
$G_q^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ enters the equations of motion.

Let $G:O\to\mathbb R^k$ be a $C^2$ regular holonomic constraint with $G_q(t,q)$ of rank $k$ on
$O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]), and
let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite. Fix $(t,q)\in O$ and write
$V=\ker G_q(t,q)$ for the virtual displacements. Then:

1. for every $R\in\mathbb R^n$, the condition $R\cdot\delta=0$ for all $\delta\in V$ holds if and
   only if there is a unique $\lambda\in\mathbb R^k$ with

$$R=G_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T}\lambda ;$$

2. the $k\times k$ matrix

$$C(t,q):=G_q(t,q)M^{-1}G_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T}$$

   is symmetric and positive definite, hence invertible; in particular for every $R$ orthogonal to
   $V$ the multiplier of clause 1 is $\lambda=\bigl(G_qM^{-1}G_q^{\mathsf T}\bigr)^{-1}G_qM^{-1}R$,
   and the multiplier is a $C^1$ function of $(t,q,R)$.

Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, let $G:O\to\mathbb R^k$ be of
class $C^3$ with $G_q(t,q)$ of rank $k$ for every $(t,q)\in O$ (a regular holonomic constraint,
[[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]), let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric
positive definite, and let $f:O\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$. Define, for
$(t,q,v)\in O\times\mathbb R^n$,

$$C(t,q):=G_q(t,q)M^{-1}G_q(t,q)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \Lambda(t,q,v):=-C(t,q)^{-1}\Bigl[G_qM^{-1}f+G_{tt}+2G_{tq}[v]+G_{qq}[v,v]\Bigr],\qquad a(t,q,v):=M^{-1}\bigl(f+G_q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda\bigr),$$

where all terms in the bracket are evaluated at $(t,q,v)$, and
$2G_{tq}[v]:=\sum_i2\partial_t\partial_{q_i}G\,v_i$ and
$G_{qq}[v,v]:=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_jG\,v_iv_j$. Then:

1. $C$ is symmetric positive definite and $C^{-1}$, $\Lambda$ and $a$ are of class $C^1$ on
   $O\times\mathbb R^n$; in particular $a$ is locally Lipschitz in $(q,v)$;
2. through every $(t_0,q_0,v_0)\in O\times\mathbb R^n$ there is a unique maximal solution
   $(q,v):I_{t_0}\to O\times\mathbb R^n$ of the first-order system

$$q'=v,\qquad v'=a(t,q,v) ;$$

3. if the data satisfy the consistency conditions

$$G(t_0,q_0)=0,\qquad G_t(t_0,q_0)+G_q(t_0,q_0)v_0=0,$$

   then the maximal solution satisfies $G(t,q(t))=0$ and
   $G_t(t,q(t))+G_q(t,q(t))q'(t)=0$ for all $t\in I_{t_0}$; consequently $q$ is an
   ideal-constraint motion of $(G,M,f)$ with multiplier $\lambda(t)=\Lambda(t,q(t),v(t))$, and
   its reaction $R=G_q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda$ satisfies the power identity

$$R(t)\cdot q'(t)=-\Lambda(t,q(t),v(t))\cdot G_t(t,q(t)) ;$$

4. conversely, every $C^2$ ideal-constraint motion $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ of $(G,M,f)$ whose velocity
   is permitted solves this first-order system with $v=q'$; hence the ideal-constraint motions
   with permitted velocity are exactly the solutions of the system with consistent data.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Adopt the force branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$ labels
with masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, a nondegenerate open time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
and a force map $F$ with the standing regularity
([[def-cm01-configuration]], [[def-cm01-units]]). Fix one inertial frame with
adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ and write $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})\in\mathbb R^{3N}$
with coordinate velocity $w=x'$ ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]).

**(a) Velocity-constraint datum.** A **velocity-constraint datum** on this
data is a quadruple $(O_{v},k',A,b)$ with:

1. an **ambient set** $O_{v}\subseteq I_{0}\times Q$, open and nonempty;
2. an integer $k'$ with $1\le k'\le 3N-1$;
3. maps $A:O_{v}\to M_{k'\times 3N}(\mathbb R)$ and
   $b:O_{v}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ of class $C^{2}$
   ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of declared dimensions
   chosen so that every row satisfies $[A_{\alpha j}w_{j}]=[b_{\alpha}]$ —
   the output of each row of the law below is a single declared quantity;
4. the **constant-rank hypothesis**: $A(t,x)$ has rank $k'$ for every
   $(t,x)\in O_{v}$, equivalently the linear map
   $A(t,x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ is surjective
   ([[def-linear-map]], [[cor-matrix-rank-nullity]]).

The **constraint law** of the datum is
$$A(t,x)\,w+b(t,x)=0 .$$

**(b) Admissible velocities, virtual displacements, admissible curves.** For
$(t,x)\in O_{v}$ the **admissible velocities** are the vectors
$v\in\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0$. They form the nonempty affine
subspace $v_{0}+\ker A(t,x)$ (nonempty because $A(t,x)$ is surjective), with
direction the linear space
$$V(t,x):=\ker A(t,x)\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \dim V(t,x)=3N-k'$$
by rank-nullity ([[cor-matrix-rank-nullity]]). The elements of $V(t,x)$ are
the **virtual displacements** of the datum at $(t,x)$: the admissible
velocity differences at frozen time and configuration, in the Chetaev
prescription of [[def-cm-nonholonomic-velocity-constraint-law]]. A
**kinematically admissible curve family** is a map $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$
on an interval $J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]])
such that $(t,x(t))\in O_{v}$ and
$A(t,x(t))x'(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ for every $t\in J$; its velocity at each time is
admissible by definition.

**(c) d'Alembert velocity-constraint model.** A **velocity-constraint model**
consists of the force-branch data, a velocity-constraint datum $(O_{v},k',A,b)$
and the declaration that the labels' motion satisfies the constraint law
while a reaction field acts: a **motion** of the model is a kinematically
admissible curve family $x:J\to Q$ together with a continuous reaction field
$R:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ of force dimension satisfying
$$\mathsf M\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)+R(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $\mathsf M$ the mass operator of [[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (d).
The model is a **d'Alembert model** when, in addition, the reaction is
**ideal**: along every motion,
$$R(t)\cdot\delta=0\qquad\text{for every }\delta\in V\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)=\ker A\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),$$
the pairing being the Euclidean inner product ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).
This is the **adopted idealization** of the mechanism that realizes the
velocity constraint — the analogue for velocity constraints of the ideal
reaction law of the holonomic branch — and it is not a consequence of the
constraint being imposed. By the multiplier lemma
([[lem-linear-functional-annihilating-kernel-of-a-surjection-is-a-transpose-multiple]]),
applied at each time to the surjective $A(t,x(t))$, the ideal condition holds
at time $t$ if and only if there is a unique $\mu(t)\in\mathbb R^{k'}$ with
$$R(t)=A\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\mu(t);$$
the representation is a mathematical consequence of the condition and the
rank hypothesis, while the ideal condition itself is the adopted part. The
equation of the d'Alembert model in multiplier form is therefore
$\mathsf Mx''=F+A^{\mathsf T}\mu$ along an ideal motion.

**(d) Holonomic equivalence and nonholonomic models.** The datum is
**holonomic-equivalent** on $O_{v}$ when there exist a $C^{2}$ map
$\Phi:O_{v}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $\Phi_{x}$ of rank $k'$ on $O_{v}$ and a
$C^{2}$ map $\varrho:O_{v}\to GL(k',\mathbb R)$
([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) with
$$A(t,x)=\varrho(t,x)\,\Phi_{x}(t,x),\qquad b(t,x)=\varrho(t,x)\,\Phi_{t}(t,x)\qquad\text{on }O_{v};$$
for a physical datum, each component $\Phi_{\beta}$ has a declared dimension
$\phi_{\beta}$. With $[x_j]=\ell$ and $[t]=\tau$, assign
$[\varrho_{\alpha\beta}]=[b_{\alpha}]\tau/\phi_{\beta}$; then every term
in the two matrix products has the declared dimension of the corresponding
entry of $A$ or $b$. These component assignments are part of the model's
declaration.
The datum is **locally holonomic-equivalent at a point** when such a pair exists on some open neighbourhood of that point, and **locally nonholonomic there** when no such neighbourhood and pair exists, as in [[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (e). A **nonholonomic model** in this local sense specifies a point (or region of points) with this failure. Absence of one pair on the whole domain $O_v$ alone is insufficient, since a global obstruction need not be local nonintegrability. In
the holonomic-equivalent case the law is the differentiated family of
position constraints $\Phi(t,x)=\text{constant}$: for a $C^{1}$ curve with
$(t,x(t))\in O_{v}$, the chain rule
([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) gives
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Phi\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)=\Phi_{t}+\Phi_{x}x'=\varrho^{-1}\bigl(b+Ax'\bigr),$$
so the constraint law holds exactly when $\Phi(t,x(t))$ is constant; a
holonomic-equivalent model is thus one whose constraint is equivalent to a
family of $k'$ independent position constraints with regular differentials,
presented through the nowhere-vanishing factor $\varrho$. For $k'=1$ the
factorization $A=\varrho\Phi_x$, $b=\varrho\Phi_t$ says that the one-form
$b\,dt+A\cdot dx$ is $\varrho\,d\Phi$: in this single-row case, local
nonholonomicity means that no such integrating factor and regular potential
exist on any neighbourhood of the specified point. For $k'>1$, local
nonholonomicity is defined by failure of the matrix factorization above, not
by a single one-form criterion. In a separate reduced two-coordinate model
$q=(s,\theta)\in\mathbb R^{2}$ of a disk rolling along a straight line (not
the $3N$-coordinate datum of clauses (a)-(c)), let $[s]=[a]=\ell$,
$[\theta]=1$ and $a>0$. Its no-slip law $s'-a\theta'=0$ is
holonomic-equivalent with $A=(1,-a)$, $b=0$,
$\Phi(s,\theta)=s-a\theta$ of dimension $\ell$, and dimensionless
$\varrho=1$; the velocity constraint $z'=xy'$ of
[[def-cm-nonholonomic-velocity-constraint-law]] is not: an integrating factor
would make the distribution $\ker A$ tangent to the level sets of $\Phi$, and
[[prop-cm-nonholonomic-distribution-is-not-tangent-to-level-sets]] proves
that this distribution is not tangent to the level sets of any $C^{2}$
function with nonvanishing differential. Tong's cited example is a specific
coin of radius $R>0$ rolling without slipping down a slope, with generalized
coordinates $(x,y,\theta,\phi)$ and velocity constraints
$$x'=R\phi'\sin\theta,\qquad y'=R\phi'\cos\theta,$$
where $x,y,R$ have length dimension and $\theta,\phi$ are angles in radians,
which he identifies as non-holonomic (Section 2.3.2, Eq. (2.41)). This is a
source-reported classification of that rolling-coin model; this item does not
prove it or classify all three-dimensional rolling models.

**(e) Status and scope.** The d'Alembert law of clause (c) is a prescription
for the reaction at frozen time and configuration, adopted as the physical
idealization of the mechanism; it is **not** identified with the vakonomic
(stationary augmented action) prescription of
[[def-cm-nonholonomic-velocity-constraint-law]]. For the sample model $z'=xy'$
with unit mass, zero applied force and initial data
$(x,y,z)(0)=(0,0,0)$, $(x',y',z')(0)=(1,1,0)$,
[[cex-cm-dalembert-and-vakonomic-evolutions-differ]] proves that the unique
d'Alembert motion is not vakonomic with those data. Thus the d'Alembert
solution set is not a subset of the vakonomic solution set for that datum,
and the two sets are unequal; this does not assert that a vakonomic motion
with those data exists. The closing remark of this page records the
distinction and its scope. The framework excludes from
this branch: points where the rank of $A$ drops (the multiplier system
degenerates there, and no continuation is asserted); unilateral constraints
and contact changes (a skate leaving the ground, a wheel beginning to slip),
which require their own mode-change models; impacts; dry friction along
admissible directions, which must be declared as a separate force
contribution; and active drives, whose driving is an additional force of the
model. Whether a concrete mechanism is described by this class, and whether
its reaction can supply the computed multiplier, are application-level
statements recorded with the apparatus; the definition asserts no measured
value.

derivations.claim: The M1 constraint data and its holonomic-equivalence: $\mathcal G_{q}=(1,-a)$ has rank one, $\ker\mathcal G_{q}=\{(a\delta,\delta):\delta\in\mathbb R\}$ as a set of virtual displacements, and along any admissible curve $x'-a\theta'=0$; hence $\mathcal G(q(t))$ is constant by [F4], so the constraint is the differentiated position constraint $\mathcal G=$ constant and is holonomic-equivalent in the sense of [F5].

The M1 acceleration, multiplier and reaction: by [F1] with the time-independent data of [F2], $C=\mathcal G_{q}M^{-1}\mathcal G_{q}^{\mathsf T}=\frac1m+\frac{a^{2}}{I}=\frac{I+ma^{2}}{mI}$, $\mathcal G_{q}M^{-1}\Phi=\frac{f}{m}$, and $\Lambda=-C^{-1}\frac fm=-\frac{mI}{I+ma^{2}}\cdot\frac fm=-\frac{fI}{I+ma^{2}}=\lambda$. The equations $Mq''=\Phi+\mathcal G_{q}^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ read $mx''=f+\lambda$ and $I\theta''=-a\lambda$; substituting $\lambda$ gives $mx''=f-\frac{fI}{I+ma^{2}}=\frac{fma^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}$, that is $x''=\frac{fa^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}$, and $I\theta''=\frac{afI}{I+ma^{2}}$, that is $\theta''=\frac{af}{I+ma^{2}}$; this is the displayed triple, with reaction $\mathcal G_{q}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=(\lambda,-a\lambda)$. The reaction power vanishes because $R\cdot q'=\lambda x'-a\lambda\theta'=\lambda(x'-a\theta')=0$ by the constraint, in agreement with the power identity of [F1] and $\mathcal G_{t}=0$.
The M2 acceleration: by [F3], $x''=f/m$ and $\theta''=0$.

The models disagree and the comparison is quantitative: for $f\ne0$, subtracting the two predictions gives $x''_{\mathrm{M2}}-x''_{\mathrm{M1}}=\frac fm-\frac{fa^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}=\frac{f}{m}\cdot\frac{I}{I+ma^{2}}\ne0$, so the two declared models are distinct; taking the ratio, $\frac{x''_{\mathrm{M1}}}{x''_{\mathrm{M2}}}=\frac{ma^{2}}{I+ma^{2}}=\frac{1}{1+I/(ma^{2})}$, which is $\frac{2}{3}$ at $I=\frac12ma^{2}$ and $\frac12$ at $I=ma^{2}$.

The contact capability condition: the no-slip contact can realize the ideal reaction only when the required scalar tangential force $f_s=\lambda$ lies in its declared capacity interval. Step 1.2 gives $|\lambda|=\frac{|f|I}{I+ma^{2}}$; for the uniform disk $I=\frac12ma^{2}$, this is $\frac{|f|}{3}$, so the condition is $|f|\le3\mu_{s}N$, or $|f|\le3\mu_{s}mg$ under the declared load $N=mg$. If the bound fails, the no-slip idealization is infeasible for that contact model and a separate slipping model is required; transitions between rolling and slipping — like general three-dimensional rolling and rank or contact changes — are outside the present comparison.

Finite model data: with $m=1$, $a=1$, $I=\frac12$, $f=3$ and $g=10$ one has $x''_{\mathrm{M1}}=\frac{3\cdot1}{\frac12+1}=2\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}$, $x''_{\mathrm{M2}}=3\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $\lambda=-\frac{3\cdot\frac12}{\frac12+1}=-1\,\mathrm N$, so $|f_s|=1\,\mathrm N$; with the declared $\mu_{s}=\frac12$ and $N=mg=10\,\mathrm N$, the capacity $\mu_{s}N=5\,\mathrm N$ includes the required reaction and M1 is feasible under the declared contact model. With $f=18$ instead, $x''_{\mathrm{M1}}=12\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $\lambda=-6\,\mathrm N$, whose magnitude exceeds $5\,\mathrm N$, so the required force lies outside the declared contact capability and M1's premises fail.

Clauses 1-5 are proved: the reduced ideal no-slip model and the frictionless sliding model have the displayed accelerations, they are distinct for every nonzero applied force, the ideal model's reaction is the displayed contact pair with vanishing power, and the contact capability condition selects the models on explicit data. The example is a comparison of declared reduced models, not a derivation of the disk's reduction from rigid-body mechanics and not a measurement.
